entries.description: A malformed resource identifier reaches the database unvalidated and surfaces as an unhandled HTTP 500.
entries.currentState: NEW AT §297A, FOUND BY A SINGLE AUTHORISED PROBE AND CONFIRMED IN PRODUCTION. One authenticated GET /files/<malformed> returned HTTP 500 in 313 ms. The production log names the cause exactly: QueryFailedError: invalid input syntax for type uuid. The route takes the path parameter straight to a TypeORM lookup with no shape validation, so Postgres rejects it and the resulting driver error is unhandled. WHAT WAS CHECKED BEFORE CLASSIFYING IT. The response body returned to the client is the generic {"statusCode":500,"message":"Internal server error"} — NO stack trace, NO SQL, and the supplied value is NOT echoed back. The route is behind JwtGuard, so it is not reachable unauthenticated. The probe referenced no real resource and crossed no tenant boundary. Nothing was mutated. So this is NOT an authorization bypass, NOT cross-tenant exposure, NOT sensitive-data disclosure, NOT a destructive mutation, and NOT a critical availability risk — none of the §297A mandatory-escalation categories applies, and §297A therefore registered it rather than stopping. TWO SECONDARY OBSERVATIONS. The attacker-supplied value IS echoed into the server-side log line, which is operator-side and is the caller's own input rather than customer data, but it is a user-controlled value reaching the log store. And an authenticated caller can produce cheap 500s at will, which is the one thing that makes this more than cosmetic: five of them inside five minutes would raise a real service.error_rate_exceeded and reach the operator, so this defect is also a route to manufacturing alert noise. §297B REPRODUCED IT FIVE MORE TIMES TO EXERCISE THE MONITORING THRESHOLD, AND THAT DOES NOT MAKE IT ACCEPTABLE BEHAVIOUR. Six genuine unhandled 500s have now been observed on this path in production. The defect is unchanged, its severity is unchanged, and it was deliberately NOT repaired while it was being used as an instrument — repairing the stimulus while validating the layer downstream of it would have destroyed the only confirmed qualifying condition the product has. It must not be read as normal endpoint behaviour, and the monitoring closure does not depend on it remaining broken: any qualifying error-severity condition reaches the same path. §303 SCOPED IT AND CLOSED IT. The first act of §303 was to measure the family rather than special-case the reported route: 24 GET routes carrying an identifier path parameter were probed with 7 malformed shapes (168 probes) against a live authenticated application. EIGHT routes across FOUR controllers returned HTTP 500 on malformed input — storage (GET /files/:id, the originally reported route), canonical reports, inspection and sites. The §297A remediation note predicted exactly this ('the same pattern is likely') and it was correct. The repair is an INPUT BOUNDARY, not an error handler: a single shared ParseUUIDPipe instance (backend/src/common/uuid-route-param.ts) is attached to the 25 route parameters that are genuinely compared against a uuid column, so malformed syntax is refused with 400 BEFORE any query is issued. No QueryFailedError is caught, and no driver error is reclassified. All 8 routes now return 400 on all 7 malformed shapes. PROVEN LIVE IN PRODUCTION AT §303. Deployed 9242d157 on both halves and read back from /health five consecutive times before creating anything. Authenticated: all 8 previously-affected routes returned 400 with an identical product-owned body carrying no SQL, no driver name, no schema and no echo of the input. Unauthenticated malformed returned 401, not 400. Valid-but-absent returned 404 on every route, uppercase UUID was accepted, and a real site created through the product path round-tripped at 200. monitoring.serverErrorsInWindow read 0 before, 0 after and 0 at the end, lastDelivery null — no service.error_rate_exceeded alert, because no server error was produced. §303 manufactured no new 500s to demonstrate monitoring, which it forbade. ONE HONEST LIMIT: the full "1' OR '1'='1" string never reached the application in production — the Cloudflare edge in front of Render returned 403 with an HTML body. That is a different layer and is not evidence about this repair; the application-level claim rests on a'b, ;drop and 1--2, which do reach the application and return the product 400, and on the disposable-database suite, which drives the full string with no edge in the path.
entries.evidence: Production probe 2026-09-14T23:43:56Z, HTTP 500, 313 ms. Render log store, same second: "QueryFailedError: invalid input syntax for type uuid". Generic client body confirmed from the response bytes. §303: verification/current/se5-malformed-identifier-303/ — pre-repair measurement (8 routes x 500), post-repair measurement (40/40 assertions, 0 failed), and the live production proof.
entries.remediation: Validate the identifier shape before it reaches the query — a UUID pipe on the route parameter, returning 400 — or catch the driver error and return 404 so a malformed identifier is indistinguishable from an absent one. The second is the better default on a route that reads by id, because it also avoids confirming which identifiers are well-formed. Audit sibling routes that take an id path parameter: this route was probed, the others were not, and the same pattern is likely.
entries.retestRequirement: GET /files/<malformed> returns a contained 4xx and raises no operational event; a valid-but-absent id still returns 404. §303 DURABLE GATE: npm run test:303-malformed-identifier, wired into hazlenz:integration:inner and therefore into hazlenz:precommit. It was watched to FAIL before the repair (the pre-repair log is retained), so it is evidence and not decoration. 41 assertions, 0 failed. It measures the input-boundary claim in BOTH directions: with storage_objects renamed away, a VALID id returns 500 (genuine faults are not swallowed) and a MALFORMED id returns 400 (no query is issued before rejection, since any query at all would have failed).
entries.note: Deliberately NOT repaired in §297A. The section authorised using an existing fault as monitoring evidence and repairing it only if it prevented safe completion or created a critical exposure; neither applies. It is also NOT a Threshold-B blocker: it needs an authenticated account, discloses nothing, and changes no state, so it does not stand between the product owner and their own internal use. §297B: classification preserved unchanged. The alert payload it produced carries path "/files/:id" and failureKind "QueryFailedError" and does NOT contain the malformed identifier, so using it as an instrument disclosed nothing. §303 CLOSURE LIMITS, STATED PLAINLY. (1) The pipe is NOT applied to every parameter named id: /auth/verify-invite/:token carries an opaque varchar token and the ParseIntPipe :version route keeps its own contract, both asserted. (2) The repair does NOT move the security boundary — a pipe runs after guards, so an unauthenticated malformed request is still 401, and a cross-tenant well-formed id is still 404; both asserted. (3) A genuine persistence failure is STILL 5xx: the suite renames storage_objects out from under a live query and requires 500, which is what stops this repair from degenerating into 'all QueryFailedError = 400'. (4) Uppercase hexadecimal is accepted as valid UUID syntax, so the fix invents no new client-facing failure.

entries.description: The migration history does not describe the invitation-to-organization relationship it must: 1779000000000 declares invitation."organizationId" as character varying against organization."id" uuid, so on any database BUILT FROM MIGRATIONS the relation join is invalid SQL and invitation verification returns HTTP 500 for every token.
entries.currentState: CORRECTED AND RE-SCOPED AT §304. §303 REGISTERED THIS AS A PRODUCTION DEFECT AND THAT WAS WRONG. §304 measured live production directly, read-only: invitation."organizationId" is ALREADY uuid there, it already carries a foreign key to organization(id), and GET /auth/verify-invite/<unknown token> answers 404 — not 500. The route works in production and always did. WHY THE TWO DISAGREE. Production's invitation table was created by TypeORM synchronize BEFORE migrations were baselined over the existing schema, and synchronize inferred uuid correctly from the @ManyToOne. Its constraint names prove the origin: PK_beb994737756c0f18a1c1f8669c and FK_5c00d7d515395f91bd1fee19f32 are TypeORM-generated, whereas the hand-written migration names its constraints PK_invitation_id and UQ_invitation_token. §303 observed the 500 on a DISPOSABLE database — which is a migration-built database — and generalised it to production without probing production. THE DEFECT IS REAL AND IS NOT COSMETIC. Every disposable verification database gets the broken shape, so every integration suite runs against a schema production does not have; and any environment ever rebuilt by replaying migration history — a new region, a restore that replays rather than loads a dump, a fresh staging — would get an invitation feature that 500s on every token. A migration history that does not describe production is also the thing that makes 'we can rebuild from migrations' untrue. §304 ALSO MEASURED HOW WIDE THAT DRIFT IS: 36 column-type divergences, 21 tables present only in production, 19 columns only in production and 6 only from migrations. Exactly TWO of the 36 are the uuid-vs-varchar class — invitation."organizationId" and user."organizationId" — and only the first is exercised by any current query. The rest is registered separately as SE-12. MIGRATED AND DEPLOYED AT §304. A fresh production backup was taken and CONTENT-VERIFIED before the migration (78/78 tables identical after restoring into PostgreSQL 17.11). The upgrade path was proven on that verified restore first: 78 tables before and after, the only table with changed content was "migrations", and NO column changed — the conversion branch correctly skipped because production was already uuid. Production then read back: 56/56 applied, head 1800000024000, organizationId uuid, FK_invitation_organization ON DELETE RESTRICT, uq_invitation_token present, relation join executes, 78 tables, 0 invitation rows. entries.description: The migration history does not describe production: 36 column-type divergences, 21 tables present only in production, 19 columns only in production and 6 only from migrations.
entries.currentState: REGISTERED AT §304, NOT REPAIRED. Measured by building a database from the full migration history and diffing it against live production, column by column. Production was created by TypeORM synchronize and migrations were later baselined over it, so the two have never been the same schema. SE-6 is one instance of this, and it is the only one currently exercised by a query — exactly two of the 36 divergences are the uuid-vs-varchar class (invitation."organizationId", repaired by §304, and user."organizationId", which is latent because nothing currently loads the user->organization relation). The remaining 34 are varchar length bounds, timestamp with/without time zone, one enum, one integer, one text and one jsonb-vs-array. The 21 production-only tables include the already-registered 'outcomes' (DB-4) and a legacy 'users'/'report' set alongside the canonical 'user'/'reports'. §305A: SE-12 IS NOT DEFERRED, AND §305A FOUND ITS FIRST PROVEN BETA-v1 CASUALTY. Driving the complete individual workflow on a migration-built database, ACCOUNT DELETION FAILED WITH HTTP 500: `relation "notifications" does not exist`. The Notification entity is live and AuthService.deleteAccount deletes from it, but no migration creates the table. Production has it — it is in the production-only list — so deletion works there, and §303 and §304 both exercised it live at 200. So this is not a production outage; it is proof that a rebuilt environment loses a core individual-product function and a data-protection obligation. CLASSIFICATION (§305A requirement): 82 divergent objects classified A/B/C/D — A(Beta v1 individual) 18, B(deferred Company/Team) 1, C(shared infrastructure) 47, D(retired/unknown) 16. Exactly ONE object is Company/Team, which settles the question of whether SE-12 could be deferred with the team feature: it could not. EIGHTEEN of the 21 production-only tables HAVE A LIVE ENTITY, so application code can reach tables no migration creates. The Beta v1 workflow nonetheless completed to an issued report without 20 of the 21. §305 CLOSED IT. ONE CANONICAL VERSIONED SCHEMA CONTRACT now exists: backend/src/database/canonical-schema.manifest.json, 68 tables, digest 3a51b1a21294f40649a57ab0f0857fb2816e5e695a7cabe35c05043b9185bf60, generated FROM a fresh migration replay so it is by construction a statement about the migration history. Scope classes: ACTIVE_INDIVIDUAL_BETA 18, SHARED_INFRASTRUCTURE 46, DEFERRED_COMPANY_TEAM 3, RETIRED_COMPATIBILITY 1. Convergence migration 1800000025000 converges from EITHER side — no-op where production already holds canonical state, repair everywhere else. THREE-WAY PROOF, MACHINE-COMPARED: (1) empty database -> all migrations -> manifest, 0 material differences, digest reproducible across independent replays; (2) restored current production -> pending convergence -> manifest, 0 material differences; (3) entity contract checked against the converged schema. THE PROVEN CONSEQUENCE IS REPAIRED: DELETE /auth/me now returns 200 on a migration-built database, where §305A measured 500 (`relation "notifications" does not exist`).
entries.evidence: verification/current/se6-invitation-relationship-304/03-PRODUCTION-VS-MIGRATION-SCHEMA-DIFF.json, produced by diffing a freshly migration-built database against live production read-only. §305A: verification/current/beta-v1-scope-305a/SE-12-OBJECT-CLASSIFICATION.json (82 objects, A/B/C/D with the basis for each) and scripts/test-305a-individual-beta-scope.ts assertion F-1. §305: verification/current/se12-canonical-schema-305/ — watched-to-fail artifact (68 material differences against pre-§305 history), backup content proof (78/78 tables identical), manifest summary, and the individual workflow run on BOTH a fresh migration-built database and an upgraded production restore (55 assertions each, 0 failed).
entries.remediation: A deliberate reconciliation programme, not a single migration: decide for each divergence whether production or the migration history is correct, write forward migrations for the former and correct the history's description for the latter, and add a gate that fails when a migration-built schema and production disagree. That gate is the durable part — without it the drift simply resumes. §305: durable gate `npm run check:canonical-schema` builds a fresh database from migrations, extracts the normalized schema through the single shared extractor in src/database/canonical-schema.ts, and fails on material drift. Wired into hazlenz:precommit. Constraint and index NAMES are normalized away — production's synchronize-generated names and a migration's hand-written names describe the same key — so the gate reports material differences only, which is what SE-12's whole history says was missing.
entries.retestRequirement: A schema-diff gate reports zero divergences between a database built from migration history and production, and is proven to fail when one is introduced.
entries.note: This is the reason SE-6 could be registered as a production outage at §303 and be wrong: nobody could tell whether a disposable database's behaviour predicted production's. It also makes 'rebuild from migrations' an unproven claim. Related to DB-4. Not a Threshold-B blocker; production itself is consistent and serving. §305A raised this to P0. Rebuild reliability, disposable-verification validity and disaster-recovery confidence are not Company/Team concerns, and the account-deletion failure shows the individual product is already affected. It is also the reason §303 could register SE-6 as a production outage and be wrong: nothing could tell whether a disposable database predicted production. §305 CLOSURE LIMITS, STATED PLAINLY. (1) Production retains RETIRED_COMPATIBILITY tables and two tolerated legacy columns (user.password, user.legacy_id); they are preserved deliberately, named in the extractor, and excluded from enforcement — so production's raw digest is NOT equal to the manifest digest, while the MATERIAL comparison over enforced scope is 0 differences. (2) Pre-existing entity-versus-database contradictions remain and are registered separately as SC-2: six standards_master columns the entity declares and no database has, and timestamp-versus-timestamptz mismatches on several tables. Both exist identically in production AND in a fresh replay, so neither affects rebuild equivalence, which is what SE-12 is about.

entries.description: CROSS-TENANT DISCLOSURE, CONFIRMED IN LIVE PRODUCTION. An authenticated user with no organization received another tenant's organization settings from GET /organization/me/settings, because TypeORM drops a `where` condition whose value is null and the query became unfiltered.
entries.currentState: FOUND, CONFIRMED IN PRODUCTION AND CONTAINED AT §305A. OrganizationsService took the caller's organization id straight from the session. An individual has none, so the value was null — and TypeORM 0.3 DROPS a where condition whose value is null rather than rejecting it. `findOne({ where: { id: null } })` therefore executed as `SELECT ... LIMIT 1` with NO WHERE CLAUSE and returned an arbitrary organization; `find({ where: { organizationId: null, status: 'active' } })` kept only the status and matched every active membership in the database. PRODUCTION PROOF: a freshly registered individual account with organizationId null called GET /organization/me/settings against live production and received HTTP 200 with a real company-plan workspace — id, name, planCode, riskProfileId, logoPath and createdAt. The account was removed immediately afterwards and no other tenant's data was retrieved or retained; the organization name and id are redacted in the evidence. REACHABILITY, WHICH DIFFERS PER ROUTE. GET /organization/me/settings carries JwtGuard ALONE — any authenticated account could reach it, with no entitlement and no role. GET /organization/me/members and /me/invites additionally require the teamMembers entitlement, so they needed a paid or promotional account; members exposes membership rows WITH the joined user records, and invites exposes invitation rows including invitee email addresses and INVITATION TOKENS, which are membership-granting credentials. Production holds 8 organizations and 8 memberships and ZERO invitations, so settings and members were live-disclosable and no token could be disclosed. WHY IT SURVIVED THIS LONG. The obvious test — an individual against an empty organization table — returns 404 and looks correct. The disclosure only appears once another tenant exists. §305A's own first run passed this section against an empty table and failed the moment the same code ran after §261 and §304 had left organizations in the shared disposable database. CONTAINED, DEPLOYED AND RE-PROBED AT §305A. Production now serves 4063434b and GET /organization/me/settings returns 401 {"message":"Organization context is required."} to an individual with no organization — the same probe that returned HTTP 200 and a real company-plan workspace before the fix. The individual product was re-verified live on the same release (site create 201, read-back 200, SE-5 malformed identifier still 400) and the synthetic account removed through the product path. SCOPE OF THE PRODUCTION VERIFICATION, STATED EXACTLY: /organization/me/settings was verified DIRECTLY in production, and it is the one that mattered most because it carries JwtGuard alone and was reachable by any authenticated account. /organization/me/members and /organization/me/invites could NOT be exercised in production, because they sit behind the teamMembers entitlement, no promotional code is configured in the production environment, and creating a paid account would have meant a commercial charge. They are verified by the §305A suite with a PRO individual and a planted foreign tenant — both return 401 and disclose nothing — running the identical deployed code. They are additionally unreachable in production today without a paid subscription.
entries.evidence: §305A live production probe (redacted) returning HTTP 200 and a foreign company-plan organization to an individual with organizationId null; §305A suite section D, which now plants a foreign tenant — 1 organization, 1 member, 1 invitation — before asserting, so the case cannot pass vacuously again.
entries.remediation: CONTAINED AT §305A by the convention this repository already uses everywhere else: `reports`, `classifications`, `reviews` and `control-verifications` each resolve scope through a `requireOrganization(user)` that throws when the scope is absent. OrganizationsService was the only service that took the same value and trusted it; it now refuses a missing scope in findOne, getMembers, getInvitations, createInvitation and (through findOne) updateSettings. This widens no guard, grants no one access and builds no deferred functionality — a caller with no organization is refused, which is what should always have happened.
entries.retestRequirement: npm run test:305a-individual-beta-scope, section D: with a foreign tenant present, an individual with no organization receives 401 'Organization context is required.' from settings, members and invites, and nothing belonging to the foreign tenant appears in any response body. Closes when the containment is DEPLOYED and re-probed in production.
entries.note: THIS IS THE CASE §305A'S OWN RULE WAS WRITTEN FOR: 'Do not automatically close a security issue merely by declaring its feature deferred.' Company/Team functionality is deferred, but the route was exposed, authenticated and disclosing live data, so the defect is ACTIVE and not FEATURE INCOMPLETE. It is also a THRESHOLD-B concern, not only Threshold C: it discloses the product owner's own workspace to any authenticated account. It remains OPEN until deployed — the repair exists in the candidate, not yet in production. RELATED CLASS: the same TypeORM null-drop hazard exists wherever a possibly-null session value feeds a where clause. §305A scanned for it; the four other services already guard, and the route-parameter cases are protected by §303's UuidParam, which rejects a non-UUID before it can reach a query.

entries.description: Two services decoded the JWT by hand and read claims this product does not sign, so their scope predicates were undefined and TypeORM dropped them — returning every user's notifications, and every tenant's audit log.
entries.currentState: FOUND AND CONTAINED AT §305 during the SE-13 generalization sweep. NotificationsService and AuditController each decoded the token as `{ sub, tenantId, role }`. `signAccessToken` signs NEITHER `sub` NOR `tenantId` — it signs `userId` and `organizationId` — so both values were undefined on every request, and §305A had already established what TypeORM 0.3 does with an undefined value in a where object: it DROPS the predicate. NOTIFICATIONS: findMine became `find({ where: {} , take: 50 })` — the 50 most recent notifications of ALL users — and markRead became `findOne({ where: { id } })`, so any notification was readable AND mutable by id, with the saved row returned to the caller. Behind JwtGuard plus the cloudReports entitlement. AUDIT: `/audit` is MOUNTED (AuditModule is imported transitively by classifications, corrective-actions, reviews and taxonomy) and getAuditByTenant(undefined) became `find({ where: {}, take: 100 })` — the 100 most recent audit rows of every tenant. WHAT WAS AND WAS NOT EXPLOITABLE. The notifications table is EMPTY in production, so nothing was disclosable — but that is a coincidence maintained by a second bug, not a control, and it stops holding the moment a corrective action creates a notification. The audit route was unreachable for a different accidental reason: it requires `['owner','admin'].includes(auth.role)`, and the signed role is either an OrganizationRole (member, manager, organization_admin) or `individual` — none of which match. That is the SAME vocabulary mismatch registered as SE-9. Repair SE-9 and the audit route begins disclosing every tenant's audit trail the same day. CONTAINED, DEPLOYED AND PROVEN AT §305. The durable proof is the §305A suite’s NON-VACUOUS isolation gate, which §305 added precisely because SE-13 hid behind an empty table: user B is given a REAL notification and B’s ability to see it is asserted BEFORE A’s inability. A cannot read it (absent from a 200 list), cannot mark it read (401), and B’s row is genuinely untouched; /audit discloses no other tenant’s rows; and when B deletes their account the ON DELETE CASCADE foreign key §305 added removes the notification with it. PRODUCTION VERIFICATION SCOPE, STATED EXACTLY: /notifications and /audit could NOT be exercised in production, because both sit behind paid entitlements (cloudReports, auditTrail), no promotional code is configured there, and creating a paid account would mean a commercial charge. They are verified by the suite on the identical deployed code and are unreachable in production today without a paid subscription.
entries.evidence: §305 sweep of 39 scope predicates; production probe confirming /audit is mounted (401, not 404); JWT payload inspection confirming neither `sub` nor `tenantId` is signed.
entries.remediation: CONTAINED AT §305. Both now read the claims the product actually signs, REFUSE when no identity is present, and derive the tenant exactly the way CorrectiveActionsService derives it when it WRITES these rows — `tenantId || organizationId || user:<userId>` — so reads and writes agree for an individual, who has no organization. The audit route's role check is left exactly as strict as it was; widening it would be building deferred Company/Team authorization, which §305 forbids.
entries.retestRequirement: An individual and a second user each hold notifications; neither can read or mark read the other's. Closes when deployed and re-probed.
entries.note: Same root cause as SE-13 in two more places, which is why §305 swept for the class rather than fixing one site. The sweep covered 39 where-objects built from possibly-null authority values; the other candidates were already guarded — reports, classifications, reviews and control-verifications each resolve scope through requireOrganization, inspection.assign refuses before querying when the inspection has no organization, and corrective-actions wraps its membership lookup in an explicit organizationId check. Route-parameter lookups are additionally bounded by §303's UuidParam, which rejects a non-UUID before it can reach a query.

entries.description: Pre-existing entity-versus-database contradictions that exist identically in production and in a fresh replay: six standards_master columns the entity declares and no database has, plus timestamp-versus-timestamptz mismatches on several tables.
entries.currentState: REGISTERED AT §305, NOT REPAIRED. entries.description: AuthService.deleteAccount wraps its transaction in a bare `catch {}` that discards the cause and rethrows a generic 500, so an account-deletion failure reaches no log and no operator.
entries.currentState: FOUND AT §305A while diagnosing the account-deletion 500. The catch takes no error binding at all, so the underlying `relation "notifications" does not exist` reached neither the Nest exception logger nor the operational event stream. The message had to be recovered by temporarily instrumenting the service. The route does record the reason in a security audit row, which is the right instinct, but that row is not where an operator looks when a customer reports that they cannot delete their account. Contrast canonical-reports.service.ts, which emits report.generation_failed with a failureKind AND stores the message — that is the pattern this should follow. CLOSED AT §305. The catch now binds the error and emits `auth.account_deletion_failed` carrying the failure KIND and an accountPreserved flag — no message, no identifier, no SQL — the same discipline report.generation_failed already follows. The client contract is unchanged: the caller still receives the generic message. PROVEN AGAINST A REAL FAULT: the §305A suite renames the notifications relation away, drives a real deletion, and asserts the 500 discloses nothing while exactly one event reaches the operator with failureKind QueryFailedError, and that the account survives intact rather than half-removed.

entries.remediation: Bind the error, emit an operational event carrying the failure KIND (not the message, which can contain identifiers), and keep the audit row. Do not log the message itself.

entries.description: The employer-pro promo code is inert: registration reports planCode "pro" and promoApplied true, and the very next login resolves the account to free with fullSafeScope false.
entries.currentState: FOUND AT §300 WHILE ATTEMPTING THE HZ-9 PROOF, AND MEASURED END TO END IN PRODUCTION. POST /auth/register with a configured promo returned 201, planCode "pro", promoApplied true; the JWT minted at the next login carried planCode "free", effectivePlanCode "free", subscriptionStatus "none", billingEntitlements.fullSafeScope false; POST /hazlenz/classify returned 402 PAID_SUBSCRIPTION_REQUIRED. ROOT CAUSE, TWO FAULTS COMPOUNDING: (1) AuthService.resolveSessionContext calls getBillingStatus({userId, email, planCode, type}) and does NOT pass user.subscriptionStatus, although the promo registration deliberately writes subscriptionStatus "active" onto the user row next to planCode "pro"; (2) in getBillingStatus, `normalizeStripeSubscriptionStatus(...) || (fallbackTier === "free" ? "none" : "active")` has an UNREACHABLE right-hand branch, because normalizeStripeSubscriptionStatus ends in `return "none"` and never returns a falsy value. The branch exists precisely to treat a paid tier carrying no explicit status as active. So fallbackStatus is always "none", resolveAccessTier("pro","none",null) returns "free", and effectivePlanCode — which prefers billingSnapshot.tier — discards the user row's "pro". NO CUSTOMER IS AFFECTED TODAY: EMPLOYER_PRO_PROMO_CODES was empty in production before §300 and is empty again after it, so no promo account has ever existed in production. The defect is latent, not live. §301 — ROOT CAUSE CONFIRMED EXECUTABLY AND REPAIRED. The §300 summary was right and is now proven rather than read: normalizeStripeSubscriptionStatus was exercised over undefined, null, empty, whitespace, garbage and every valid status and returns a NON-EMPTY STRING IN ALL CASES, so the `|| (fallbackTier === "free" ? "none" : "active")` alternative in getBillingStatus is DEAD FOR EVERY POSSIBLE INPUT. The PROXIMATE cause is one omission: resolveSessionContext called getBillingStatus with { userId, email, planCode, type } and withheld subscriptionStatus, although the promo registration deliberately writes it. With the status withheld the resolver read "none" and resolveAccessTier("pro","none",null) returned free. THE REPAIR IS THE OMISSION: resolveSessionContext now passes user.subscriptionStatus. The dead alternative was DELETED rather than made reachable — making it live would mean "any account whose TIER claims pro is treated as ACTIVE even though nothing says its subscription is", an entitlement WIDENING derived from a caller-supplied field in the one function every feature gate consults. Deletion is provably behaviour-preserving because the left side is total. SECURITY: repairing BI-4 does NOT create public self-escalation. dto.planCode and dto.selectedPlan are declared on RegisterDto and NEVER READ by the service; the only non-free branch at registration is a promoCode matching EMPLOYER_PRO_PROMO_CODES, a SERVER ENVIRONMENT allowlist a registering user cannot write to, and a non-matching code is REFUSED with 400 leaving no account behind. PROVEN END TO END through the real HTTP path on a disposable database (35 assertions, 0 provider calls): an ordinary registration is free and classify refuses it 402; a promo registration is pro, a FRESH LOGIN STILL RESOLVES PRO — the exact step where §300 measured free — and classify returns a deterministic classification; requesting planCode pro or selectedPlan pro yields free and 402; guessing the promo yields 400 and no user row; active grants entitle, expired and revoked grants do not; a fresh session after revocation is free; tenant B is unaffected by tenant A's grant; and with the allowlist emptied the same code that worked is refused. The suite also reproduces the PRE-REPAIR resolution on the very same account row, so it distinguishes repaired from never-broken. 42 further unit assertions cover the precedence matrix and a durable source-level anti-self-promotion guard.
entries.remediation: DONE at §301. Propagate subscriptionStatus; delete the dead widening branch. No billing redesign, no migration.

entries.description: Revoking an entitlement grant does not take effect for a session that was already issued: EntitlementService.hasFeature returns on the JWT tier claim before it reaches the grant lookup, so an existing access token retains paid capability until it expires.
entries.currentState: FOUND AT §301 WHILE PROVING BI-4, AND MEASURED RATHER THAN INFERRED. With no UserSubscription row, hasFeature takes its else-branch and returns TRUE on normalizeBillingTier(user.planCode) from the JWT — which, for a grant-entitled account, the server itself minted as "pro" because getBillingStatus applied the grant at login. The grant lookup further down is never reached. MEASURED: a token minted before revocation still received HTTP 201 from POST /hazlenz/classify after the grant was set to revoked, while a FRESH login for the same account correctly resolved free and was refused 402. THIS IS RETENTION, NOT ESCALATION — the token cannot gain anything it was not issued with, tenant isolation is unaffected, and a fresh session always re-derives authority from server state. The window is bounded by JWT_EXPIRES_IN, which defaults to 15 minutes. CONSEQUENCE FOR OPERATIONS: revoking a grant is not an instant kill switch for live sessions, so any cleanup that must prove capability is gone has to verify with a FRESH login rather than by replaying the old token — which is what the §301 proofs do. §302 — CLOSED FOR GRANT-DERIVED AUTHORITY, which is the case EN-2 was measured on and the case EN-3 depends on. A revocation that waits for a token to expire would have made §302's bounded, revocable grant hollow, so the session now records HOW its tier was reached (entitlementBasis, minted by the server) and a grant-derived session declines to answer from the JWT claim, letting the live grant lookup decide. MEASURED: the §301 integration case that returned 201 on a pre-revocation token now returns 402, and §302 case J-1 asserts it directly. NOT WIDENED: organization-seat plans are carried purely on the JWT with no row to check against and are unchanged; tokens minted before §302 carry no basis and keep the previous path, so the change cannot retroactively lock out a live session. WHAT REMAINS OPEN is the same staleness for authority that is NOT grant-derived — an organization-seat claim still rides on the JWT for up to JWT_EXPIRES_IN (15 minutes by default) — which is the standard bearer-token trade-off and is now the whole of this entry. §305A: the grant-derived half was closed at §302. What remains is the ORGANIZATION-SEAT half, which §305A defers with Company/Team functionality — it has no effect on individual Beta behaviour, because an individual holds no seat. §305A proved individual entitlement remains server-authoritative: a free individual is refused 402 and a promotional individual resolves pro from a bounded grant whose basis the canonical billing route names.

entries.description: A promo-granted plan is PERMANENT and has no product-controlled revocation: it writes planCode/subscriptionStatus onto the user row, and removing the allowlist does not downgrade accounts already promoted.
entries.currentState: FOUND AT §301 WHILE PERFORMING THE REQUIRED CLEANUP. The two entitlement mechanisms are asymmetric. An entitlement_grant is bounded (startsAt/endsAt), revocable (status), attributed (issuedByUserId) and audited — §301 proved revocation removes capability from a fresh session. The PROMO path writes planCode=pro and subscriptionStatus=active directly onto the user row with NO expiry, NO status field of its own, and NO product route that lowers it: there is no downgrade endpoint, and DELETE /auth/me destroys the whole account rather than the entitlement. CONSEQUENCE: emptying EMPLOYER_PRO_PROMO_CODES stops NEW promotions but leaves every already-promoted account on pro indefinitely. §301 cleanup therefore had to delete the synthetic accounts rather than revoke their entitlement, which is a blunter instrument than the grant path offers and is not available at all for a real customer. §302 — REPAIRED. A promotion is now a BOUNDED ENTITLEMENT GRANT and the account row stays truthful. NO MIGRATION: entitlement_grants already carried everything needed, so §302 reuses it rather than inventing a fourth representation of what plan an account is on. THE CALLER DECIDES NOTHING: buildPromotionalGrant receives the id of the account just created and nothing from the request; the module reads no dto field, has no request-shaped input, takes source and tier from constants, and takes the duration from server environment. DURATION: the product defined none — the only rule anywhere was the admin route's 90-day CEILING for human-issued operational grants, which is a limit rather than a recommendation — so 7 days, configurable by PROMOTIONAL_GRANT_DAYS and CLAMPED at 30 because §302 forbids exceeding that without a product-owner decision; a value above the ceiling is clamped and says so, and anything unparseable, zero or negative falls back to the default rather than producing an already-expired or infinite grant. BILLING TRUTH: the account row records free/none, and the temporary capability is reported separately as promotionalEntitlement naming basis bounded_entitlement_grant, so nothing claims a purchase that did not happen. REAUTHORIZATION: the promo applies only at registration, is invoked from exactly one place, and a repeat registration on the same email is refused before anything is created — measured, the account still holds EXACTLY ONE grant with an unchanged expiry, so there is no self-service perpetual-renewal path. PROVENANCE WITHOUT SECRETS: source, tier, bounds and how the duration resolved are recorded in the grant and in a promotional_entitlement_granted audit event; the promo code appears in neither, nor in the registration response. PROVEN: 45 gate assertions and 41 integration assertions through the real HTTP path, the headline ones being that a revoked grant leaves THE ACCOUNT ABLE TO LOG IN while resolving free, and that a token issued BEFORE revocation is refused AFTER it without a new login. LIVE PRODUCTION PROOF COMPLETE. Deployed at 61828222 (backend dep-dakspd61egvs73bp6fvg, frontend dpl_EDeigrCvLxS3mttyhL2p6d2AGFiz), 0 migrations, schema unchanged. ONE synthetic account through the public registration route: the account row came back FREE while promotionalEntitlement reported tier pro expiring in ~259 seconds; a fresh login resolved pro with entitlementBasis grant and fullSafeScope true; and /hazlenz/classify returned 201 with a real analysis at riskBand Critical. AFTER THE GRANT EXPIRED — through the product's own bound, with no database write, no platform-admin operation and no account deletion — the token issued inside the window was refused 402 WITHOUT a new login, THE ACCOUNT STILL LOGGED IN, and its fresh session resolved free / basis none / fullSafeScope false with classify 402. That is the property this entry exists for: at §301 the only way to remove promotional entitlement was to delete the account. OPS-2 DID NOT RECUR: a non-mutating probe — the promo code sent with the agreement deliberately omitted, which the server refuses before any write either way — was polled to five consecutive stable answers before the account was created AND again before testing removal, so no orphan was possible. 0 direct production DB writes, 0 charges, 0 platform-admin operations, 0 Expert executions, 0 provider calls, $0. Environment restored byte-identical (43 keys); the synthetic account is left in place as §302 permits — free, no capability, and the subject of the proof.
entries.remediation: DONE at §302. Promotions issue a bounded entitlement_grant; the account row is no longer written. No migration, no billing redesign.
entries.retestRequirement: npm run test:302-promotional-grant (in hazlenz:test) and test:302-promotional-grant-integration (in hazlenz:integration:test).
entries.note: Registered, not repaired: §301 scope discipline permits repairing another defect only if it directly prevents a secure BI-4 repair. It does not — BI-4 is repaired and proven, and cleanup was completed by account deletion. It does mean the promo path is unsuitable as the long-term pilot/internal entitlement mechanism, which is the question §301 asked and this is the answer to it.

entries.currentState: MECHANISM IMPLEMENTED AND PROVEN; NO DESTINATION CONFIGURED IN PRODUCTION. §291 built the push half MO-1 asks for: every error-severity operational event is dispatched to a configured destination, repeated 5xx raise ONE service.error_rate_exceeded rather than one alert per request, and one alert per event kind per 15-minute window keeps an outage from becoming a mail storm. Proven against a real induced storage failure: six consecutive 500s produced THREE alerts — one per event kind plus one rate alert — while 401, 404 and 400 produced none, which is the noise policy §291 specified. §291 did NOT invent a production destination, because choosing an alerting channel has a cost and an account attached. /health/ready now reports alerting: NOT_CONFIGURED, so "nothing is watching" is a visible fact rather than a silent assumption. THIS IS NOT YET MONITORING IN PRODUCTION. §292 SEARCHED FOR AN EXISTING DESTINATION AND FOUND NONE. Project documentation names exactly one established operational destination — the Render service notification (notifyOnFail, email to the workspace owner) — and that is a PLATFORM channel for deploy and service failure that the application cannot publish into. There is no Slack, PagerDuty, Sentry or webhook configuration anywhere in the repository or either platform; Render has zero webhooks and no log stream; and the Resend credential that would enable the email channel does not exist (EM-2). §292 did NOT invent a destination. The noise policy was re-proven on the §292 build against a real receiver: 401, 404, 400, duplicate-register and 402 produced ZERO alerts, while one qualifying 500 produced two alerts — one per event kind — delivered in 4 ms with metadata carrying no content. §293 RE-VERIFIED THE ABSENCE INDEPENDENTLY AND FOUND THE REMEDIATION INSTRUCTION UNDERSTATED. The 41 production environment variables were read again: OPERATIONAL_ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL, OPERATIONAL_ALERT_EMAIL and RESEND_API_KEY are all still absent, Render still has zero webhooks and slackEnabled false, Vercel still has zero marketplace integrations and zero storage stores, and no Resend credential exists anywhere in the repository or in standard client configuration locations. /health/ready still reports alerting: NOT_CONFIGURED. §293 additionally read the dispatch path and found that the email channel needs a THIRD variable the remediation did not name — see MO-2 — so the remediation text below is corrected rather than repeated. §294 REPAIRED THE CHANNEL BUT COULD NOT CONFIGURE IT. The false-green path MO-2 described no longer exists: setting the two variables the register used to name now leaves /health/ready reporting NOT_CONFIGURED with the missing sender named, rather than reporting a configured channel that delivers nothing. MO-1 itself is untouched by that, because no destination, credential or sender was supplied and none was invented. Production configuration is unchanged. §295 DEPLOYED THE HARDENED BUILD AND FOUND THAT THE OWNER BOUNDARY IS LARGER THAN §293 STATED. The §294 candidate is live on both halves at 87491ed9 and /health/ready serves the three-state contract, still reporting NOT_CONFIGURED. The remaining work was recorded as "name a destination and supply a credential", and for the EMAIL architecture the owner selected that is incomplete: Resend sends only from a domain VERIFIED IN THE ACCOUNT, verification is DNS records on a domain the owner CONTROLS, and the Vercel account holds ZERO custom domains — the product is served from safety-insite.vercel.app, whose apex vercel.app belongs to Vercel and cannot be verified by this owner. No Resend session exists in the owner's browser either, so no account is evidenced. The email path therefore needs a domain BEFORE it needs a credential. The WEBHOOK path needs none of that, and §293's instruction not to prefer a webhook "merely to obtain a faster green gate if an approved Resend configuration is now available" does not bite, because one is not available. The choice between them is now a genuine product decision rather than a shortcut, and it is recorded in the §295 runbook. §296 SELECTED THE ARCHITECTURE AND PROVED THE BRANCH, AND STILL COULD NOT CLOSE. The product owner chose the WEBHOOK architecture — deliberately, and not on cost or speed: the product name is to be replaced before external beta, and a verified sending domain is exactly the infrastructure that entrenches a name, whereas a webhook URL is one environment variable to replace. §296 then found that the webhook branch had never been executed since §294 rewrote the dispatcher: §291 and §292 proved it against a local receiver BEFORE the rewrite, and §294's gate proved the new outcome machinery entirely on the EMAIL branch — the string "webhook" does not appear in it. Closing MO-1 on an unexercised code path would have been closing it on the same kind of assumption MO-2 was, so the branch was proven first: npm run test:296-webhook-channel, 15/15, 0 network, 0 provider calls. WHAT REMAINS IS A DESTINATION, AND IT IS STILL AN OWNER ACTION. §296 searched the already-authorised surface for a monitored receiver and found none: there is no Slack session and no workspace (the sign-in page asks for a workspace URL), no Discord session, and none of GitHub, Render, Vercel, Neon or Stripe offers an inbound receiver that accepts an unauthenticated POST and surfaces it where a human looks. Inventing a URL, standing up an ephemeral receiver, or pointing the channel at something nobody reads were all forbidden and would each have produced a green gate over nothing watching — which is precisely the failure MO-2 was. §297A CONFIGURED THE DESTINATION, PROVED THE RECEIVER, AND STILL COULD NOT CLOSE — FOR A REASON THAT IS THE PRODUCT WORKING. The webhook destination is configured in production and /health/ready now reports alerting CONFIGURED, channel webhook, lastDelivery null. The receiver was proven reachable out of band: one hand-sent message, clearly labelled as NOT a product alert, was accepted by the destination, retrieved independently through a subscriber poll, and confirmed RENDERED IN THE OWNER'S SUBSCRIBED CLIENT. Then one authorised probe produced a GENUINE unhandled production 500 (SE-5). AND IT CORRECTLY RAISED NO ALERT. The §291 noise policy encodes that a single 500 is a bug report and a burst is an outage: service.error_rate_exceeded fires only when 5 server errors occur inside 5 minutes. After the probe, production reported serverErrorsInWindow 1 against a threshold of 5, lastDelivery null, and the destination still held only the out-of-band message. So the live chain cannot be completed by a single 500 — not because anything is broken, but because the aggregation policy is doing exactly what it was built to do. §297A forbade repeating the probe, forbade lowering the threshold to make the test easier, and forbade falling back to breaking storage without a new decision. All three were respected. WHAT IS NOW KNOWN THAT WAS NOT: every link in the chain is independently proven except the trigger. Configuration truthfulness, destination reachability, subscriber receipt and human visibility are all evidenced live; the webhook branch's dispatch and outcome recording were proven at §296; and the quiet path is proven live, because a real 500 plus a 404 plus a 401 produced zero alerts on a CONFIGURED channel. What remains is a qualifying condition, and choosing how to produce one is a product-owner decision. CLOSED AT §297B ON ACTUAL MONITORED RECEIPT. The §297A error had aged out — production reported serverErrorsInWindow 0 after 15.5 minutes against a 5-minute window — so it was NOT counted, and a fresh sequence of exactly five requests was run against the same confirmed SE-5 path. The progression is the policy stating itself: requests 1 through 4 returned 500 with serverErrorsInWindow climbing 1, 2, 3, 4 and lastDelivery NULL at every step — four genuine production errors and not one alert. The fifth crossed the threshold and produced exactly ONE service.error_rate_exceeded, dispatched to the webhook and accepted with HTTP 200 at 2026-09-14T23:59:49.031Z, 272 ms after the monitoring event. FIVE ERRORS PRODUCED ONE ALERT, WHICH IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THE AGGREGATION. The alert ARRIVED: retrieved independently through a subscriber poll as message pzDPWfb8CuTV, and confirmed RENDERED IN THE PRODUCT OWNER'S SUBSCRIBED CLIENT. Afterwards /health/ready still reports alerting CONFIGURED, channel webhook, and lastDelivery DELIVERY_ACCEPTED status 200 — the configuration remained truthful through the dispatch rather than only before it. THE TRANSMITTED PAYLOAD WAS RECONFIRMED ON THE ACTUAL BYTES, not on a local reproduction: 311 bytes carrying source, event, severity, at, environment, release and five metadata fields — path "/files/:id", method, statusCode, countInWindow and failureKind "QueryFailedError". The malformed identifier that CAUSED the errors does not appear anywhere in it, because path is the ROUTE PATTERN and failureKind is the error CLASS NAME rather than its message. That is the §268 redaction working on live production data.

entries.description: The email alert channel reports itself configured without a deliverable sender, and the delivery result is discarded, so a rejected alert is indistinguishable from a delivered one.
entries.currentState: NEW AT §293, FOUND BY READING THE DISPATCH PATH RATHER THAN BY RUNNING IT. Three limbs, all in backend/src/observability/operational-alerts.ts. (1) describeAlertConfiguration() returns configured: true, channel: email on OPERATIONAL_ALERT_EMAIL and RESEND_API_KEY alone, but dispatchOperationalAlert() sends from: PASSWORD_RESET_FROM_EMAIL || 'alerts@safety-insite.invalid'. The .invalid TLD is reserved by RFC 2606 and can never be a verified Resend sending domain, so with only those two variables set every send is rejected while /health/ready reports the channel as configured. That inverts the §291 guarantee that made MO-1 defensible — "nothing is watching" being a VISIBLE fact rather than a silent assumption — because alerting: configured would then mean nothing is watching. (2) Both the webhook and email branches are void fetch(...).catch(() => undefined) with no logging of a non-2xx response. Not throwing is correct and is the same rule §287 applied to the audit write; not RECORDING is not, and it means an unverified domain, a revoked key or a suspended account produces no signal inside the product. (3) The §291 and §292 alert proofs both ran against a local HTTP webhook receiver. No committed harness exercises the email branch at all, so the channel the owner selected at §293 has zero executed coverage. CLOSED AT §294 ON EXECUTABLE PROOF, BEFORE ANY CREDENTIAL EXISTS — which is the only order in which this defect could be closed honestly, because a configured channel would have hidden it. Three structural repairs. (1) resolveEmailChannel() is now the ONE place that decides what the email channel requires, and describeAlertConfiguration() and dispatchOperationalAlert() are both written in terms of it, so they cannot state different requirements — the parity is structural rather than a convention a later edit is trusted to keep. (2) There is NO fallback sender. alerts@safety-insite.invalid is gone and nothing replaced it: an absent or structurally undeliverable sender leaves the channel NOT_CONFIGURED with the sender named as the reason. Undeliverability is tested by reserved TLD (RFC 2606 .invalid/.example/.test and RFC 6761 .localhost/.local) rather than by naming one retired string, so the next such address is caught too, and the same rule is applied to the RECIPIENT. (3) Dispatch is still launched and abandoned with respect to the customer request — never awaited, and it still cannot turn a succeeded operation into a 500 — but the promise now resolves into evidence rather than into undefined: every attempt produces exactly one of DELIVERY_ACCEPTED, PROVIDER_REJECTED, NETWORK_FAILURE or MALFORMED_RESPONSE, emitted as monitoring.alert_delivered (info) or monitoring.alert_delivery_failed (warning). Both are deliberately below error severity so the dispatcher cannot alert about its own failure through the channel that just failed. /health/ready gained a third state, DEGRADED, for a configured channel whose last attempt did not succeed; service readiness is unaffected in all three states, because a mail provider having a bad ten minutes must not stop Safety InSite serving inspections. SENDER SEMANTICS — option A, shared, with an optional override: monitoring uses PASSWORD_RESET_FROM_EMAIL by default so one verified domain serves both monitoring and EM-2, and OPERATIONAL_ALERT_FROM_EMAIL overrides it if operations mail should ever be distinguishable. No new REQUIRED configuration was introduced and the owner still supplies three values. §296 EXTENDED THE PROOF TO THE OTHER BRANCH. §294 proved the outcome machinery entirely on the email channel; §296 proved it on the webhook channel — all four bounded outcomes, DEGRADED and recovery, dedupe and ceiling, containment, the quiet statuses through the real ServerErrorAlertFilter, and the measured wire payload. It also recorded one deliberate asymmetry: the webhook branch does NOT apply the email branch's MALFORMED_RESPONSE rule, because an arbitrary receiver has no acknowledgement schema, so 2xx IS the acknowledgement. Discord answers 204 and Slack answers 200 with the body "ok"; a dispatcher that required a JSON acknowledgement would have reported every successful Slack delivery as a failure.

entries.description: A Render deploy reports status "live" before the previous instance stops serving, so a configuration read-back taken immediately after can measure the OLD configuration.
entries.currentState: OBSERVED AT §301, AND IT PRODUCED A REAL SIDE EFFECT. The §297 rule is change -> deploy -> read the live configuration back. §301 removed EMPLOYER_PRO_PROMO_CODES, deployed, saw the deploy report status "live", and immediately registered an account with the removed code — which SUCCEEDED and was promoted, because the request reached an instance still holding the old environment. A second attempt shortly afterwards correctly returned 400 "Invalid promo code". The service record showed the variable absent throughout. CONSEQUENCE: that one read-back created a live pro account in production whose password was not retained, which had to be neutralized directly (see the §301 return). THE RULE IS NOT WRONG, THE READ-BACK IS: a single probe after "live" is not sufficient evidence that a configuration change has taken effect everywhere. §302 DEMONSTRATED THE PREVENTION WITHOUT REPAIRING THE REGISTER ENTRY. The remediation this entry asks for — poll to a stable answer rather than sampling once, and never use a probe whose success path writes — was applied in practice: a NON-MUTATING discriminator (the promo code sent with the agreement deliberately omitted, which the server refuses before any write whichever way it goes) was polled to five consecutive identical answers before the synthetic account was created and again before testing the removal. No mixed-version serving was observed and no orphan was created. The entry stays OPEN because the practice has not been made a standing rule or a reusable helper; §302 scope discipline permitted repairing another defect only if it prevented a safe EN-3 proof, and following the practice was sufficient.
entries.remediation: Strengthen the §297 read-back: poll until the expected post-change behaviour is observed, or until a timeout, rather than probing once. For a REMOVAL specifically, prefer a probe that is safe to repeat and creates nothing on success — and never one whose success branch writes a row.
entries.retestRequirement: A configuration read-back that polls to a stable answer rather than sampling once.
entries.note: Recorded because it is a trap that will recur on every future configuration change, and because the §301 read-back is exactly the shape that is dangerous: a probe whose SUCCESS path creates production state.

entries.description: Production has no Resend credential, so password reset cannot deliver.
entries.currentState: PASSWORD_RESET_PROVIDER=resend in production, but RESEND_API_KEY and PASSWORD_RESET_FROM_EMAIL are both ABSENT from the 41 production environment variables. checkProductionConfiguration() is written to require all three, yet the service starts — so the check is not enforced as a boot refusal. Consequence: a user who forgets their password cannot recover it. It also removes the most obvious destination for MO-1 alerting. §292 checked for an already-owned credential rather than creating one: no RESEND_API_KEY in any local env file, none in the environment, and none in production. Configuring it would require creating an account and accepting terms on the owner's behalf, which §292 forbids. Left OPEN. It does not block Threshold B — password reset is recoverable for an internal owner — but it does block the email option for MO-1. §294 DID NOT CLOSE THIS AND DID NOT EXERCISE IT — no credential exists and no real password-reset mail was sent. What §294 did do is make the monitoring channel share the password-reset sender by default, so the single configuration step the owner will perform (credential plus one verified sender) serves both paths without a second architectural decision. isStructurallyDeliverableAddress is exported for the password-reset sender to use at EM-2 closure rather than growing a second, differently-wrong copy of the same test. §296 DELIBERATELY LEFT THIS OPEN AND RECORDED WHY, because the reason is a product decision rather than a deferral. The owner chose the webhook architecture for monitoring specifically so that NO permanent email or domain infrastructure is established before the product is renamed. A webhook cannot deliver a password-reset link, so EM-2 is untouched by MO-1's eventual closure and must not be read as partially satisfied by it. Transactional email will be addressed after the brand decision, or when Threshold C forces it, whichever comes first. The §295 runbook's Option B remains written and unexecuted for that day, and §294's shared-sender design means it is still one configuration step rather than an architectural rewrite. §306 FINISHED AND PROVED THE SOFTWARE PATH, AND FOUND IT WAS NOT MERELY A MISSING CREDENTIAL. EM-2 had been carried as 'production has no Resend credential', which sounds procurement-shaped; §306 was told not to assume the implementation was correct because of that framing, and it was not. THE DEFECT THAT MATTERED: resetPassword was a read-modify-write with bcrypt at 12 rounds in the middle. Two concurrent completions of the SAME token both returned 'Password reset successful' while only ONE of the two passwords actually worked — so one caller was told they had set a password they had not. Repaired by claiming the token in a single conditional UPDATE that matches and clears it and returns the affected row; Postgres serialises concurrent updates to one row, so exactly one caller wins and the loser gets the same refusal an invalid token gets. The password is hashed AFTER the claim, which also stops every invalid-token attempt paying for a bcrypt round. ALSO REPAIRED: delivery outcomes were indistinguishable internally (a bare catch discarded the error — the OB-1 shape again); the provider WAS the abstraction, so Resend is now one transport behind an interface and auth logic references it nowhere; the brand was baked into the email subject and body and now comes from PRODUCT_NAME; readiness reported nothing about email capability and now reports CONFIGURED / NOT_CONFIGURED / DEGRADED with the missing variable names, reading only whether variables are PRESENT; and the 30-minute expiry was written twice, which is how an email comes to promise a window the server does not enforce. WHAT WAS ALREADY RIGHT AND IS NOW PROVEN: 256-bit tokens, digest-only storage verified by recomputation, bounded expiry, byte-identical generic responses for known/unknown/case-variant addresses plus a timing comparison, reset-path password strength equal to registration, immediate session death via passwordChangedAt and refresh-token revocation, configuration-only reset URLs immune to Host-header injection, and throttling. 51 assertions, 0 failed, ZERO emails sent.

entries.remediation: SOFTWARE: complete. OWNER: the remainder is configuration and is brand-dependent, which is why §306 did not do it — a sending domain established under the temporary name would have to be torn down. After brand lock: register the domain, create and DNS-verify the provider sending domain, choose a sender address, and set RESEND_API_KEY and PASSWORD_RESET_FROM_EMAIL (plus PRODUCT_NAME and the reset frontend URL) in production. No code change is required to activate it.

The software path is engineering-complete and proven, but nothing has ever been delivered to a real mailbox, and §306 authorised no sending domain because the product name changes before external Beta and permanent infrastructure must not be established under the temporary brand. It still blocks external Beta: an individual Beta user who forgets their password is otherwise stuck.

entries.description: Password-reset single use was not atomic: two concurrent completions of the same token both reported success, and only one of the two passwords actually worked.
entries.currentState: FOUND AND REPAIRED AT §306. resetPassword read the user by token hash, hashed the new password with bcrypt at 12 rounds, then saved — a read-modify-write with a deliberately slow step in the middle, which is a generous window for a second request carrying the same token to pass the same SELECT. Measured against the pre-§306 logic: '2 of 2 succeeded (201/201)' with '1 of 2 passwords work'. The losing branch is the serious part: a confirmation screen saying the password was reset, and a password that does not work. Exploitability is low — it needs the victim's live reset token — and that is not the point: single use is a stated property of a reset credential, and a property that holds only when nobody races it is not a property.
entries.evidence: §306 watched-to-fail artifact run against the pre-§306 reset logic.
entries.remediation: Claim the token in ONE conditional UPDATE that matches and clears it and returns the affected row; Postgres serialises concurrent updates to the same row, so exactly one caller observes a row. Hash the password after the claim.

entries.note: The assertion checks WHICH PASSWORD WORKS rather than counting 200s: two successes that both set the same password would look harmless and are not.

entries.currentState: NEW AT §298, MEASURED END TO END IN PRODUCTION. Risk is computed at deterministic reconciliation time, and no finding is reconciled from any Expert analysis by design — so a finding created by finalizing an Expert-cited review has riskSnapshot NULL. The §298 report printed that finding as 'Not rated' with 'APPLICABLE STANDARD: Not established for this specific finding', while the deterministic finding naming the same hazard printed Critical, severity 5, likelihood 4, risk score 20, with a corrective action. THE TRACE FIRST: the provider carries no severity by contract; admission admits STRUCTURE and rates nothing; settlement settles the conclusion, not the risk; the report prints "Not rated", says so in the summary and invents nothing. THE DEFECT SITE is finalizeFindingFromReview, whose `riskSnapshot: dto.riskAssessment ? withReviewerConfirmedRisk(...) : null` had a SILENT else-branch — nothing anywhere distinguished "a reviewer decided they cannot rate it yet" from "the workflow never asked". RISK AUTHORITY: computeFindingRisk (governed, but keyed to a DETERMINISTIC decomposition hazard, which an Expert candidate is not), withReviewerConfirmedRisk (human, attributed, already working), and Expert — NONE, correctly. THE REPAIR requires a finalization that would otherwise produce a finding rated by nobody to carry either a riskAssessment or a ratingDeferred with a reason; it is refused 400 otherwise. THE RULE IS DELIBERATELY NOT EXPERT-SPECIFIC: a finding reaching the report rated by nobody is the same problem whatever produced it, and §268 H-3 proved the deterministic create-at-finalization path exists. ORDERING: the gate runs AFTER the §265 authority gate — placed before it, a finalization §265 would have refused on authority grounds came back as a 400 about risk, the right refusal for the wrong reason; §265 L-1/L-2 caught that and it was corrected.
