entries.currentState: FOUND AT §299 WHILE RUNNING THE GATE BATTERY, AND PRE-EXISTING: it reproduces unchanged at d78150ed, the commit §299 started from, and nothing in the §299 repairs touches auth, registration or agreements. §291 (SU-1) made acceptance of internal-pre-beta-acknowledgement REQUIRED at registration, which is deliberate and correct product behaviour. §262, §264, §265, §267 and §268 each POST a registration body without acceptedAgreements, so each received 400 "Acceptance of ... is required" and then 401 on the login that followed. THIS IS A HARNESS DEFECT, NOT A PRODUCT DEFECT — the service behaved correctly throughout, and the repair does not weaken, mock or disable the §291 requirement: the harnesses now send an acceptance and the service still validates, records and would still reject a wrong or missing version. REPAIRED by deriving the acceptance from agreementsRequiredAtRegistration(), the same registry the service validates against, so a future version bump flows through with no edit — a hardcoded copy in a test is the same failure mode as HZ-5.
entries.evidence: backend/scripts/lib/registration-acceptances.ts; npm run hazlenz:integration:test now 435 assertions passed, 0 failed across §261/§262/§264/§265/§267/§268.
entries.remediation: DONE at §299.
entries.retestRequirement: npm run hazlenz:integration:test.
entries.note: Registered because a gate that has been silently broken since §291 is worth naming. No production code changed.

entries.description: §268 assertion E-2 pinned the literal schema version 1800000021000, so it failed against a readiness endpoint that was answering correctly after two later migrations landed.
entries.currentState: FOUND AT §299, behind IT-1 — §262 aborted first, so §268 had not run since §287's CorrectiveActionLifecycle and §291's AgreementAcceptance advanced the schema head to 1800000023000. /health/ready reported 1800000023000, which is correct; the test literal was stale. A PINNED SCHEMA VERSION IN A TEST MEANS EVERY LEGITIMATE MIGRATION BREAKS A GATE THAT IS SUPPOSED TO BE ABOUT READINESS, and the reflex repair is to bump the literal, which teaches nobody anything. REPAIRED by deriving the expectation from expectedMigrationTimestamps(), the same enumerator the endpoint uses, so what is asserted is the real property: readiness reports the latest migration on disk, as a concrete version rather than null. A genuine drift between the endpoint and the migrations directory still fails.
entries.remediation: DONE at §299.
entries.retestRequirement: npm run hazlenz:integration:test.
entries.note: Stale test expectation, not a production defect. No production code changed.

entries.description: §268 R-6 pinned a literal migration timestamp as one of the three it expected to be reported missing, so adding any migration made a correct readiness evaluator fail the suite.
entries.currentState: FOUND AND CLOSED AT §304. The case withholds the last three migrations from a fixture database and asserts the readiness evaluator names them. It asserted `behind.missing.includes('1800000021000')` — true only while 021000 happened to be among the last three. §304 added 1800000024000 and the assertion failed while the evaluator was entirely correct. This is the same shape as IT-2, where §268 E-2 pinned a literal migration timestamp, and the same shape as HZ-5: a second copy of a fact that nothing holds to the first.
entries.evidence: §304 hazlenz:precommit run: `FAIL R-6 it names exactly which migrations are missing [1800000022000,1800000023000,1800000024000]`.
entries.remediation: Derive the expectation from the fixture: capture `const withheld = expected.slice(-3)` and assert the reported missing set equals it. Self-maintaining as migrations are added, and STRICTER than before — it now requires all three to be named rather than one.
entries.retestRequirement: npm run test:268-operational-controls passes, and continues to pass when a migration is added.
entries.note: A verification-infrastructure defect, not a production one: no production code was changed and the readiness evaluator was never wrong. Third of its kind after IT-1 and IT-2, which is itself the signal — pinned literals in this suite family keep going stale. 64/64 after the repair.

entries.description: POST /maintenance/seed-safescope calls dataSource.synchronize(false) against the live database, contained in production only by an environment flag.
entries.currentState: FOUND AND REPAIRED AT §307. The handler runs an ad-hoc ALTER TABLE and then await this.dataSource.synchronize(false). A runtime synchronize is precisely what §305 spent a section making impossible: the canonical manifest is a statement about the MIGRATION HISTORY, and a route that lets TypeORM reconcile the live schema against entity metadata can move production off it, after which check:canonical-schema describes a database that no longer exists. TYPEORM_SYNCHRONIZE=false does not help because this is a direct call. The only thing protecting production was ENABLE_MAINTENANCE_SEED=false, so one operator setting the flag to seed knowledge would hand any authenticated account that also holds the maintenance token a schema synchronize against the live database. PROVEN IN PRODUCTION: an authenticated synthetic account driving POST /maintenance/seed-safescope received 404, disclosing nothing about what the route would have done.
entries.remediation: DELIVERED. Production is refused FIRST, ahead of the feature flag, with the same 404 the flag already produced, so the deployed service's observable behaviour is byte-identical and the flag is no longer the only thing in the way. Development and disposable databases are unaffected. Deleting the handler was rejected because it would also delete the seeding capability development uses, which is a product change §307 does not authorise.
entries.retestRequirement: K-synchronize checks the ORDER of the two refusals against the actual call site; K-synchronize-sweep proves no other module in src/ calls synchronize() at all.
entries.note: Classified material-but-contained: material because it can move production off its migration history, contained because the route was unreachable in production. The repair converts configuration containment into a code control.

entries.description: The unauthenticated readiness endpoint published the alerting thresholds.
entries.currentState: FOUND AND REPAIRED AT §307. GET /health/ready has no authentication by design, and answered with OPERATIONAL_ALERT_POLICY in full: serverErrorThreshold 5, serverErrorWindowMinutes 5, dedupeWindowMinutes 15, maxAlertsPerWindow 12, and the list of statuses that never alert (401, 402, 404, ordinary 400 validation, expected 409 conflict). Read as an attacker reads it that is a pacing guide: stay under five 5xx in five minutes, prefer 401/402/404, and nothing ever reaches a human. PROVEN IN PRODUCTION: five stable read-backs of /health/ready on the deployed release all report the policy block absent while alerting remains CONFIGURED and the schema position is still reported.
entries.evidence: backend/src/health/health.controller.ts; §307 assertions C-8, C-9, C-10; production read-back
entries.remediation: DELIVERED. The policy block is removed from the unauthenticated response. OPERATIONAL_ALERT_POLICY is unchanged and still exported; §294 and §296 assert against the constant directly, which is where a threshold assertion belongs. Nothing about what alerts, or when, changed.
entries.retestRequirement: C-8 asserts the policy is absent; C-9 asserts every operator-facing state §291/§294/§306/§268 put there is still reported.
entries.note: Deliberately KEPT: the CONFIGURED/NOT_CONFIGURED/DEGRADED state, channel, detail, lastDelivery, serverErrorsInWindow, the email capability with its missing variable NAMES, and the schema position. The variable names are already public in the source and the register, and an attacker can establish that recovery mail does not arrive simply by requesting a reset; removing them would cost the operator the one line that says what to set and buy nothing. A threshold was removed, not observability.

entries.description: POST /hazlenz/classify accepted a caller-supplied workspaceId that outranked the server-derived governance context.
entries.currentState: FOUND AND REPAIRED AT §307. The controller read body.workspaceId || context.workspaceId. §307 measured the consequence rather than assuming one and found NO disclosure: the workspaceId selects among site policies that are SHIPPED FIXTURES rather than customer rows, and probes naming a foreign organization, another individual's synthetic workspace, organizationId, tenantId and ownerUserId returned nothing belonging to any of them. The defect is authority, not disclosure: an authority-shaped field the server had stopped owning, which is the §305A/§305 defect class.
entries.evidence: backend/src/hazlenz/dto/classify.dto.ts, hazlenz.controller.ts, hazlenz.service.ts; §307 assertions C-3 and C-3c
entries.remediation: DELIVERED. workspaceId is REMOVED from ClassifyDto, so the global forbidNonWhitelisted pipe rejects a body carrying it with 400 rather than dropping it silently (§262: the rejection is structural). The controller reads context.workspaceId directly and both service sites read the server-derived value first. No client is affected: workspaceId exists in the frontend HazLenz client only as an optional TYPE member and is never assigned a value anywhere.
entries.retestRequirement: C-3 drives five authority-shaped fields and requires 400 for each; C-3c drives the SAME request without an authority field and requires success, so C-3 measures the field rather than a broken route.

entries.description: The deployed frontend returned no framing, sniffing or referrer protection.
entries.currentState: FOUND AND REPAIRED AT §307. The deployed frontend answered with exactly two headers of interest: Vercel's own Strict-Transport-Security and the §290 X-Robots-Tag. No Content-Security-Policy, no frame-ancestors, no X-Frame-Options, no X-Content-Type-Options, no Referrer-Policy, no Permissions-Policy. The application that holds the session token in localStorage (SE-2, accepted for Beta on the strength of a short token life) could therefore be framed by any origin and driven by clicks the user believed they were aiming elsewhere. SE-2's acceptance reasoning assumes the token is hard to REACH; it says nothing about an attacker who never needs to read it. PROVEN IN PRODUCTION: all six headers were read back from the deployed frontend on /, /login, /register and /inspection-workspace after the Vercel production deploy. This is a measurement, not a source assertion.
entries.evidence: frontend-next/next.config.ts; production header read-back recorded in SECTION-307-SECURITY-READINESS.json
entries.remediation: DELIVERED for framing, sniffing, referrer, permissions and opener. script-src is DELIBERATELY ABSENT: a real script policy for an App Router build needs per-request nonces, which means a middleware layer this product does not have and §307 does not authorise building, and shipping script-src unsafe-inline unsafe-eval to make a CSP header appear would be a header that looks like a control and is not one. camera=(self) rather than camera=() because field capture uses <input capture="environment">, which Chrome gates on that policy.
entries.retestRequirement: Read the headers off the deployed production response. A full script-src policy remains open as v1.1 work.
entries.note: A full script-src content policy is the remaining frontend security work and is a v1.1 item, not a Beta blocker.

entries.description: Every individual Beta principal resolves to one shared literal governance workspace, 'default'.
entries.currentState: FOUND AT §307, MEASURED, NOT REPAIRED. resolveHazLenzGovernanceContext returns user.organizationId || user.workspaceId || 'default'. The JWT strategy produces no workspaceId at all and an individual has no organization, so EVERY individual in the deployment resolves to the same literal string; HazLenzPersistenceController builds the same value. The absence does not make a predicate disappear, it collapses every individual into one shared scope, which is the same fault read the other way round. NOTHING IS DISCLOSED TODAY, and §307 measured why: the three surfaces scoped by that value (/hazlenz/persistence/audit-records and its trail and candidate routes) carry @Roles(ORG_OWNER, SAFETY_DIRECTOR, SUPERVISOR, AUDITOR, SUPER_ADMIN) and an individual's role is individual. An authenticated individual was driven at them with and without a named foreign workspace and got 403 both times. That is a ROLE gate, not a scope gate, and it is one role string away from failing. The service's own getById and updateStatus also guard with record.workspaceId && record.workspaceId !== user.workspaceId, so a record with a NULL workspaceId passes the cross-workspace check entirely.
entries.remediation: Derive an individual's workspace as user:<userId>, mirroring what CorrectiveActionsService already does for tenantId, and make the record-side guards fail closed on a NULL workspaceId. NOT DONE AT §307: that changes the workspace identity written on every future HazLenz persistence row and changes which existing rows a principal can reach, which is customer-data reinterpretation and a stop-for-product-owner decision under §307's repair authorisation.
entries.retestRequirement: A two-individual fixture proving one individual's HazLenz audit records are unreachable by another WITHOUT relying on the role gate.
entries.note: §305's own phrase for this shape was 'coincidences, not controls'. Registered rather than repaired precisely so the containment is not mistaken for a control.

entries.description: /terms and /privacy returned 200 and were still unreachable without authentication: the app shell redirects any path not in its public allow-list to /login, and the two new routes were not in it.
entries.currentState: FOUND AND REPAIRED AT §308, BY RUNNING THE PRODUCT RATHER THAN READING IT. Both routes returned HTTP 200, the backend served the correct publication state, the legal gate passed 23/23 and the acceptance suite passed 58/58 — and a browser navigating to /terms landed on /login. AppShell redirects any path not in its marketingRoutes allow-list, and the two new routes had not been added to it. A route that serves correctly and cannot be reached is not published, which is precisely the condition LG-3 was raised about. §308 requires both routes reachable WITHOUT authentication, and the registration page links to them before an account exists at all.
entries.evidence: frontend-next/components/layout/AppShell.tsx; re-driven in Chrome after the repair with both pages rendering their states and no redirect
entries.remediation: DELIVERED. /terms and /privacy added to the public route allow-list, with the reason recorded at the site so a future reader knows why they are there.
entries.retestRequirement: Load /terms and /privacy signed out and confirm no redirect to /login.
entries.note: The reason §308 drove a browser at all. Every automated signal was green and the feature did not work.
